candidates.next_evidence: Track 2026 booked load factor, net yield growth, onboard revenue per passenger, new-ship delivery timing, fuel/labor cost inflation, and whether bookings remain resilient across income cohorts.
candidates.node_relation: Direct asset owner and operator of cruise capacity; exposed to packaged-value travel demand, onboard spending, itinerary pricing, and ship-delivery capacity additions.
candidates.theme_relation: Consumer discretionary experiences; cruise vacations can capture value-conscious and higher-income leisure travel demand while supply is constrained by long ship-order lead times.

Its 2025 Form 10-K reported 2026 capacity growth expectations and yield performance, while S&P noted strong 2026 forward bookings at higher prices and roughly two-thirds of 2026 capacity booked. This maps directly to the node hypothesis that cruise capacity and packaged-value travel may be attractive chokepoints.

candidates.next_evidence: Track 2026 quarterly disclosures for LEAP deliveries, commercial engine deliveries, internal/external shop visit growth, spare-parts pricing, supply-chain commentary, and airline customer dissatisfaction around delivery or durability.
candidates.node_relation: Second-order scarce supplier to travel capacity: commercial aircraft engines, LEAP engine production, engine services, and MRO turnaround affect airline fleet availability and therefore air-travel capacity.
candidates.theme_relation: Consumer travel demand can be capacity-limited by aircraft and engine availability; GE Aerospace benefits if flight hours, engine shop visits, spare parts, and engine deliveries remain elevated.
candidates.why_include: GE Aerospace’s 2025 annual report explicitly discusses constrained aerospace supply chains, material availability, LEAP engine deliveries, engine shop visits, and efforts to reduce MRO turnaround times. This makes GE a high-quality supplier bottleneck candidate for the travel-capacity node.

candidates.next_evidence: Verify 2026 cumulative booked position versus historical ranges, net per-diem growth, onboard spend, ship-delivery pipeline, debt refinancing costs, and whether lower-income cruise demand remains positive.
candidates.node_relation: Direct cruise-capacity owner with global brand portfolio and exposure to ticket pricing, onboard spend, deposits, and fleet deployment.
candidates.theme_relation: Consumer discretionary travel experiences; Carnival is a scale cruise supplier and a direct beneficiary or victim of cruise demand, capacity discipline, and consumer budget substitution toward all-inclusive travel.
candidates.why_include: Carnival is the largest broad public cruise-capacity exposure. Its 2025 annual report described record booking trends and record year-end customer deposits, supporting inclusion as a direct candidate for the packaged-value cruise chokepoint lane.

candidates.next_evidence: Track room-night growth, gross bookings growth, take rate, merchant versus agency mix, Genius loyalty penetration, AI-search disruption risk, and regional exposure to Europe, Asia, and U.S. inbound travel.
candidates.node_relation: Demand-aggregation platform across hotels, alternative accommodations, flights, rental cars, restaurants, and travel services; monetizes travel search, conversion, merchant payments, and loyalty engagement.
candidates.theme_relation: Consumer travel platform exposure; can benefit from secular online booking penetration, cross-sell, loyalty distribution, and fragmented lodging supply even when asset owners face mixed RevPAR trends.

candidates.next_evidence: Track U.S. RevPAR by chain scale, group demand, World Cup host-city performance, Bonvoy member room-night penetration, net rooms growth, franchise fee growth, and owner economics under higher labor and financing costs.
candidates.node_relation: Asset-light global hotel brand and loyalty platform with direct exposure to RevPAR, net room growth, franchise/management fees, and event-driven lodging markets.
candidates.theme_relation: Consumer travel and lodging; Marriott maps to constrained hotel supply, loyalty distribution, group/transient travel, and World Cup or event calendar upside, while also testing whether hotel RevPAR can outpace inflation.

Its FY2025 results reported nearly 271 million Marriott Bonvoy members at year-end and guided to 2026 worldwide RevPAR growth and net rooms growth, making it a direct candidate for hotel supply and loyalty-distribution exposure.

candidates.next_evidence: Check FY2026 filings for commercial aftermarket organic growth, OEM build-rate exposure, sole-source/proprietary product mix, margin sustainability, leverage risk, and any regulatory or customer pushback on aerospace-part pricing.
candidates.node_relation: Second-order scarce supplier: proprietary aircraft components and aftermarket parts support aircraft utilization, MRO cycles, and fleet uptime.

candidates.why_include: TransDigm describes itself as a producer of highly engineered, often proprietary aircraft components critical to aircraft operation, with significant commercial aftermarket exposure. CoStar and Tourism Economics upgraded their June 2026 U.S. hotel outlook, citing stronger-than-expected demand and raising the 2026 U.S. RevPAR growth forecast to 2.8%.
evidence.source_title: U.S. Hotel Forecast Assumptions – June 2026 | CoStar

evidence.claim: Recent reporting cited Bank of America data showing U.S. cruise spending rose across income groups in the first four months of 2026 versus the prior year, supporting the hypothesis that cruises remain resilient packaged-value experiences.

Royal Caribbean's 2025 Form 10-K reported 2025 net yield growth and expected 2026 capacity growth of 6.7% versus 2025, tied to new ships including Star of the Seas, Celebrity Xcel, and Legend of the Seas.
S&P Global Ratings stated that Royal Caribbean reported good 2026 forward bookings at higher prices and had approximately two-thirds of 2026 capacity booked.
evidence.source_title: Research Update: Royal Caribbean Cruises Ltd. Upgraded

GE Aerospace reported 2025 commercial engine sales of 2,386 units, including 1,802 LEAP engines, and stated that engine deliveries increased primarily due to improved material supply.

TransDigm describes itself as a leading global designer, producer, and supplier of highly engineered aircraft components critical to the safe and effective operation of nearly all commercial and military aircraft.
TransDigm reported that approximately 55% of fiscal 2025 net sales were generated from aftermarket activity, mostly commercial and military aftermarket.

CoStar/STR/Tourism Economics projected 2026 U.S. hotel RevPAR growth and noted that constrained hotel supply growth is likely to remain the norm because of the lag between investment, construction, and opening.

Recent 2026 World Cup lodging evidence is mixed: Sports Business Journal reported an AHLA survey showing many host-city hotel bookings below expectations, while CoStar-cited data still forecast a nationwide RevPAR rise during the June-July tournament window.
evidence.source_title: Study shows World Cup host cities’ hotel reservations below expectations

memory_update.text: RCL and CCL are the cleanest direct public mappings for cruise-capacity and packaged-value travel exposure; prioritize evidence on 2026 booked position, net yields, onboard spend, and capacity additions.

BKNG and ABNB map to demand aggregation rather than owned physical capacity; they may benefit from fragmented travel supply, loyalty or repeat behavior, event-driven lodging, and online booking share, but require monitoring for AI-search and regulation risks.

MAR represents hotel brand, franchise, and loyalty distribution exposure rather than pure hotel real estate ownership; it is suitable for tracking RevPAR, Bonvoy penetration, and event-market lodging data.

The travel-experience-capacity node should be split in later layers into cruise capacity, hotel brand/loyalty distribution, alternative lodging supply, OTA demand aggregation, airlines, attractions/theme parks, ticketing, luggage, and travel payments.

Not included due to the 5-candidate limit but relevant for future passes: Expedia, Hilton, Hyatt, Choice Hotels, Wyndham, Host Hotels, Vail Resorts, Disney parks, United/Delta/American/Southwest, Live Nation, and payment/network beneficiaries such as Visa, Mastercard, and Global Payments.

World Cup lodging upside is not a settled fact. Recent sources show improved general U.S. hotel forecasts but mixed World Cup-specific booking evidence; future research should separate broad RevPAR recovery from host-city event spikes.

GE should be tracked as an aircraft-engine and MRO bottleneck candidate for consumer travel capacity; relevant KPIs include LEAP deliveries, spare parts, shop visits, material availability, and turnaround time.

TDG should be tracked as a proprietary aerospace aftermarket parts candidate; the key Serenity question is whether certification/installed-base specificity creates durable scarcity and pricing power as aircraft utilization remains high.
AER should be tracked as aircraft-capacity infrastructure rather than an airline; aircraft delivery delays and maintenance backlogs can increase the value of owned and leased fleets.
CSGP is a non-obvious data-infrastructure candidate through STR hotel benchmarking and event-market forecasting, but materiality to total CoStar revenue needs further validation.

PAC is a regulated airport-infrastructure candidate tied to tourism, cross-border travel, and possibly event-driven traffic; verify World Cup exposure by airport and route before upgrading confidence.

Cruise shipbuilding is likely a real capacity chokepoint, but the most direct shipyard suppliers are largely non-US-listed; US-listed cruise operators may be covered in a separate direct-capacity pass rather than this scarce-supplier pass.

Sabre is relevant travel-distribution infrastructure, but it was not included in the final five candidates because of market-cap uncertainty and weaker scarcity versus engines, aircraft leasing, regulated airports, and STR hotel data.
Add OSW as a high-relevance second-order cruise capacity/onboard-spend supplier; less obvious than cruise operators but directly tied to ship count, itinerary mix, and passenger utilization.
Add TRIP as an experiences marketplace and travel discovery/data asset; focus on Viator supply scale, commission economics, and traffic acquisition risk.
Add SABR as a below-$1B exception for travel booking infrastructure; high chokepoint relevance but requires stricter balance-sheet and disintermediation checks.
Add FOUR as an adjacent travel-experience payments infrastructure candidate spanning hotels, resorts, restaurants, venues, and tourist retail via Global Blue.
Add HST as lodging-capacity exposure to event-heavy and World Cup host markets; evidence currently supports market-level tracking rather than a uniform World Cup uplift thesis.
Need a separate pass for obvious leaders and direct capacity owners: RCL, CCL, NCLH, VIK, BKNG, EXPE, ABNB, MAR, HLT, WH, DAL, UAL, AAL, LUV, DIS, SIX/SEAS equivalents if eligible.
Need a separate supplier pass for aircraft leasing, airport services, luggage, fuel, hotel revenue-management software, property-management systems, and alternative accommodations data providers.

node: Travel experiences: cruises, hotels, online travel platforms, airlines, attractions, and event-driven lodging
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the direct public-company universe for travel-experience capacity. The highest-confidence candidates are cruise operators with constrained physical capacity and strong booking curves, online travel platforms aggregating lodging and experience demand, alternative-lodging supply aggregators, and asset-light hotel brand/loyalty platforms. This pass excludes weaker undifferentiated airline capacity and focuses on companies where demand aggregation, packaged-value travel, loyalty distribution, or lodging supply can plausibly create pricing power or operating leverage. Expanded universe for scarce or capacity-constrained enablers around travel experiences. The strongest chokepoint-adjacent candidates are not necessarily airlines or hotels themselves, but aircraft engine/parts suppliers, aircraft lessors, regulated airport concessions, hotel market data infrastructure, and travel distribution software. Key bottleneck themes: aircraft delivery and maintenance constraints, proprietary aerospace aftermarket parts, leased-aircraft availability, regulated airport capacity/tariff regimes, hotel supply growth lag, event-market forecasting, and GDS/travel marketplace infrastructure. Expanded universe for the travel-experience-capacity node emphasizes second-order and underappreciated chokepoints rather than only airlines, hotel brands, cruise operators, or OTAs. The strongest non-obvious mappings found in this pass are: cruise onboard monetization suppliers, experiences marketplaces, travel distribution infrastructure, hospitality/event payments, and lodging REIT exposure to cons
